title: CASE OF LĂCĂTUŞ AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for home);Violation of Article 6 - Right to a fair trial (Article 6 - Civil proceedings;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing);Violation of Article 14+6 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 6 - Right to a fair trial;Article 6-1 - Fair hearing);Violation of Article 14+8 - Prohibition of discrimination (Article 14 - Discrimination) (Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life;Article 8-1 - Respect for home)
summary: In the case of Lăcătuş and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Ms. Voichiţa (Rostaş) Lăcătuş and her daughters, Ms. Speranţa-Lămâiţa Rostaş and Ms. Rada-Codruţa Rostaş—are members of the Roma community, as defined by the Council of Europe, who brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case centred on the extreme vulnerability of Roma families subjected to violent attacks, destruction of their homes, and subsequent homelessness, compounded by the authorities’ failure to provide protection or redress. On 20 September 1993, in the village of Hădăreni, a violent confrontation led to the death of a non-Roma man, after which a mob, including police officers, attacked Roma residents. The applicants’ home was destroyed, and they were forced to flee and live in overcrowded, inadequate conditions for years, receiving no assistance from the authorities. The European Court of Human Rights examined violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life and home), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), finding that Romania had violated all these rights, both substantively and in terms of discrimination. The Court awarded remedies for the harm suffered. This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent discrimination and violence faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe, particularly in the post-communist context of the 1990s, and affirms the responsibility of states to protect minority communities from both private and institutional harm.
